transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SA), Michael Lee (Valen CISO), Hannah Ortiz (Valen Head of Cloud Infra), Raj Patel (Valen Security Engineer), Avery Kim (Valen Procurement)
Shared artifacts: redwood-private-vpc-architecture.pdf, SOC2-TypeII-redacted.pdf, sample-terraform.zip

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, and with me is Ethan, our SE, and Priya — we'll run through Private VPC security architecture and answer any compliance questions.
[00:12] Michael: Thanks, Sofia. High level, Valen is under a fairly tight compliance regime — PCI-ish workloads and SOC2, plus some ISO reqs. We want to understand network isolation, ingress/egress control, and how keys are managed for on-prem or VPC.
[00:28] Ethan: Great, Michael. We'll start with an overview — Redwood Private is deployed with a customer-controlled VPC. The control plane can be self-hosted or run- uh, run in a customer-managed project. All compute nodes live in private subnets, no public IPs by default, and we rely on VPC endpoints and NAT gateways for any outbound connectivity.
[00:45] Hannah: Quick clarification — when you say control plane self-hosted, do you mean we keep the control plane in our account or you provide a managed plane in your tenancy?
[00:52] Priya: Good q. We support both. For highest isolation you run both control and data planes in your cloud account, we provide the artifacts and automation. If you want Redwood managed control plane, we do cross-account IAM roles with strict trust, but most banks go full customer-managed.
[01:10] Raj: On key management  — can we use our HSM/KMS? We have YubiHSM and AWS KMS with HSM-backed keys.
[01:16] Ethan: Yes. We integrate with customer KMS — AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or on-prem HSMs via KMIP where supported. Secrets and model encryption keys never leave KMS; Redwood uses envelope encryption. We also support bringing your own keys with rotation policies you control.
[01:35] Michael: And are keys ever cached on node disk or in memory? Need assurance for memory-scrubbing and disk encryption.
[01:42] Ethan: Keys are not persisted in plaintext on disk. We pull ephemeral wrapping keys from KMS and keep only in process memory for the lifetime of the job; memory is zeroed on process exit, and all disks are encrypted at rest. In Linux images we recommend and support dm-crypt/LUKS or cloud provider-managed disk encryption. Sorry, that was a mouthful.
[02:05] Hannah: About ingress  — what do external API calls look like? We need to route through our firewall and WAF, ideally no public-facing endpoints.
[02:12] Sofia: For Private, the recommended pattern is an internal load balancer inside your VPC that fronts the Redwood inference service. You can put the ALB behind your corporate firewall, require mTLS with client certs or use a bastion/proxy. Optionally, Redwood can provide a small egress-only bastion if needed for patches, but most customers prefer patching via internal CI/CD pipelines.
[02:33] Raj: Egress control is my main concern — models reaching out to external registries or telemetry phoning home.
[02:38] Ethan: By default there is no telemetry that leaks PII. For model artifacts we support private model registries in your network — no public pull. Telemetry is configurable and can be disabled; when enabled it goes to endpoints you specify. We also support VPC endpoint policies to restrict allowed S3 buckets or artifact registries.
[02:58] Michael: Can you walk network flow top to bottom? From client request to inference and back.
[03:05] Priya: Sure. Client -> internal ALB (mTLS or SAML-protected proxy) -> Redwood ingress service in private subnet -> request is routed to inference pool (GPU nodes) -> nodes access model artifacts from customer S3 via VPC endpoint -> inference happens -> response returned over the same flow. Control plane management traffic uses cross-account role calls only when control plane is external. All traffic between nodes is over private subnets and encrypted in transit (TLS).
[03:32] Hannah: Do you support VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail ingestion to our SIEM?
[03:36] Ethan: Yes, we strongly recommend enabling VPC Flow Logs and sending to your central S3/logging account or to a SIEM like Splunk/Datadog. We push audit events to a customer-configured logging bucket as well — these include job start/stop, user actions via the console, and admin operations.
[03:50] Michael: How granular are audit logs? I need user-level actions, role changes, and API calls for compliance.
[03:55] Sofia: Audit logs include user identity (SSO/SAML or IAM principal), action, timestamp, and resource. We can retain the logs for the duration you require; longer retention is an add-on.
[04:05] Raj: If we need to correlate with our SIEM, do you support structured logs (JSON) and syslog forwarding?
[04:10] Ethan: Yes, structured JSON logs and you can forward via Kinesis/Firehose or syslog connectors. We also support an event-stream to a Kafka endpoint in your VPC for advanced integrations.
[04:22] Michael: About SSO and RBAC  — we use Okta SAML and SCIM provisioning. Can Redwood map our groups to roles?
[04:28] Sofia: Absolutely, we integrate with Okta/SAML/OIDC and support SCIM for user provisioning. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles and enforce SSO-only access. RBAC supports fine-grained roles and resource-level policies.
[04:40] Hannah: Any default service accounts or do we have to create them?
[04:44] Ethan: We recommend creating dedicated service accounts in your cloud account with least privilege. Our Terraform samples create minimal IAM roles/policies; you can tighten them further.
[04:53] Raj: Firewalling  — do you need open egress to update agents or pull images?
[04:58] Priya: No, we support air-gapped and restricted egress modes. For fully restricted environments, you can host a local artifact registry and container image store. For updates we provide signed bundles that can be pulled via an approved pipeline. For managed updates, a narrow set of egress IPs can be whitelisted. We'll provide the list if you want managed patches.
[05:18] Michael: What about network segmentation for multi-tenant deployments? Valen will run multiple business units; we need strong tenant isolation.
[05:24] Ethan: For multi-tenant we recommend separate VPCs or separate subnets with strict security groups and node isolation. We also support dedicated capacity pools per tenant — physically separate GPU nodes where required.
[05:36] Raj: Does Redwood support FIPS 140-2 modules for crypto? We may need that for certain workloads.
[05:41] Ethan: We have FIPS-compatible modes for TLS stacks and can work with FIPS-certified KMS/HSM. It's a supported pattern but may require additional validation depending on your environment.
[05:53] Hannah: Can you describe how ingress is authenticated? We prefer mutual TLS between client services and Redwood endpoints.
[05:59] Priya: mTLS is supported. We also recommend putting an API gateway in front that does SAML/OIDC auth and then mTLS to internal services. You can also use client certs issued by your internal CA and rotate them via your PKI.
[06:12] Michael: Data residency  — we have EU customers. Can we specify region for both control and data planes?
[06:18] Sofia: Yes, you pick the region for data plane, and for control plane as well if you're self-hosting. We can deploy into your preferred cloud region and ensure logs and artifacts remain in-region.
[06:28] Raj: Regarding backups and snapshots  — are they encrypted and how are they stored?
[06:32] Ethan: Disk snapshots and backups are encrypted using your KMS keys where supported. We never store unencrypted model weights in the Redwood-managed buckets. Backups go to the customer-managed S3 or equivalent, optionally with MFA-delete enforced.
[06:45] Avery: From procurement perspective, we need the SOC 2 report and an ISA. Is that something you can provide under an NDA?
[06:50] Sofia: Yes, we'll send a redacted SOC2 Type II and our security whitepaper after the call. We'll include the pen test summary under NDA.
[06:58] Michael: One important ask  — we have strict egress rules: only certain hosts and ports allowed; can Redwood support egress via a proxy with credentials?
[07:05] Ethan: We support proxy egress with auth. Our agents can be configured to go through a corporate HTTP proxy with mutual auth or token-based auth. For deeper controls, you can host a local artifact mirror.
[07:17] Hannah: Can you run through a minimal IAM policy for AWS that gives the runtime just what it needs?
[07:22] Priya: Sure — at a high level: allow s3:GetObject on specific buckets/prefixes, kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey on the specified CMK, ec2:Describe for metadata calls, ssm:GetParameter if you're using Parameter Store for secrets. No wildcard s3:* in the samples; we'll share the exact Terraform snippet.
[07:43] Raj: Do you support network-level eBPF or host-based IDS integration? We run Falco.
[07:49] Ethan: We don't ship host IDS, but you can run Falco on hosts and collect kernel events; Redwood doesn't block that. We also emit OS-level audit events to your logging account.
[07:58] Michael: How about vulnerability scanning of container images?
[08:02] Sophia: small correction, Priya: we recommend scanning images prior to onboarding. Redwood verifies image signatures and you can integrate Clair/Trivy in your CI. We also provide a hashed manifest of runtime images for attestation.
[08:20] Raj: For the pilot, we want to validate latency and that nothing tries to phone home. We also want a proof of key handling. Can we do a short runbook?
[08:28] Ethan: Yes — pilot runbook: deploy Private in a test VPC, enable VPC Flow Logs + CloudTrail to your SIEM, provision KMS CMK with rotation off for controlled test, point inference at a small model, run traffic, and verify logs. We'll help instrument with perf counters and token-level tracing.
[08:44] Michael: Any SLA differences for Private versus Hosted?
[08:47] Sofia: Private SLAs are contract-negotiated; Dedicated has SLA targets too. For Private we typically do availability target based on your infra, but Redwood supports operational runbooks and 24/7 support add-ons.
[08:59] Hannah: One more — how do you handle patching the inference runtime without breaking pinned model versions?
[09:04] Ethan: We support canary rollouts and immutable images. Pinned model versions remain valid across runtime versions. We also keep backward compatible serving for common workloads; if a breaking change is needed we coordinate a migration window.
[09:18] Priya: Quick note on firewalling: Security groups are least-priv, NACLs are stateless but used for extra guardrails; we recommend security groups + NACLs + WAF at perimeter. Bastion for admin access with jumpbox and session recording.
[09:32] Michael: This has been helpful. Let's recap next steps?
[09:36] Sofia: Recap — we'll send SOC2 and architecture doc, Ethan will share terraform and network diagram, Valen will send egress list and KMS preference, and we'll schedule the pilot kickoff.
[09:49] Avery: From procurement, we'll need a draft SOW and estimated pricing for a 3-month pilot and for dedicated capacity.
[09:55] Sofia: We'll put together an initial SOW and pricing and include options for Dedicated vs Private.
[10:02] Michael: Thanks all.
[10:05] Ethan: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:09] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("Sofia" transcribed as "Sofie" in a few places in automated copy), some technical terms abbreviated (KV cache written as "K V cache" in earlier auto transcript).
